questions.text: Can every member of the executive team state, in the same words, why this transformation is happening and what success looks like in 12 months?
In the last leadership meeting, did leaders resolve at least one contested trade-off (scope, budget, sequencing) on the record rather than deferring it?
Do leaders publicly connect their own decisions and priorities to the transformation, or is it delegated to the programme team?
Is there a named executive sponsor who attends programme reviews personally and can commit resources without escalating further?
Does the governance forum review adoption and readiness evidence — not just milestones, budget and RAID logs?
When the programme conflicts with business-as-usual priorities, is there a documented escalation path that produces a decision within days, not months?
Have you mapped every affected stakeholder group and recorded, group by group, their current level of support, resistance or uncertainty?
Can you name the groups most likely to work around the new system or process, and do you know why?
Are influential informal leaders — not just formal managers — identified and actively engaged in each affected area?
For each role that changes, have you assessed what people can actually do today against what the new way of working requires?
Is training designed around real transactions and scenarios from each role's daily work, rather than generic system walkthroughs?
Do you measure proficiency after training (observed or assessed performance), not just attendance and completion?
Are the future-state processes documented at the level of who does what, in which system, with which handoffs — and signed off by the business owners who will run them?
Have process exceptions and local variations been surfaced, decided and documented, rather than left for users to discover at go-live?
Have the highest-volume processes been rehearsed end-to-end with real data before go-live?
Have representative end users — not only super-users — completed hands-on practice in the new system before go-live?
Is there a plan, with owners, for retiring the legacy tools, spreadsheets and workarounds the new system replaces?
Will you be able to see, from system data, who is transacting in the new system and who is not — role by role, week by week, after go-live?
Does every affected group hear what is changing for them specifically — their tasks, their deadlines, their support — not only programme-level announcements?
Is communication two-way, with questions and objections logged, answered and visibly influencing the plan?
Are messages sequenced around what each audience needs at each stage, rather than broadcast on the programme's reporting calendar?
Have frontline and middle managers been equipped — before their teams — with what to say, what to model and how to handle resistance?
Do managers have a simple routine (huddle questions, check-ins, escalation route) for reinforcing the new way of working in daily operations?
Are managers themselves measured and supported on adoption in their teams, or only on delivery output?
Have you defined, before go-live, the adoption metrics that will prove the change is being used — and the business outcomes they are expected to move?
Is readiness and adoption evidence reviewed on a fixed cadence, with named owners for acting on what it shows?
When measurement shows adoption stalling, is there a funded intervention path (coaching, redesign, re-training) rather than more communication?
Do people affected by the change believe it will make their work better — and can they say why in their own words?
Is it safe in this organisation to say 'this isn't working' about the change — and does saying so lead to help rather than blame?
Have past change failures been acknowledged honestly, with visible lessons applied to this programme — or do people expect this one to fade like the last?

anchors.4: Established — practised and evidenced in most areas
anchors.5: Embedded — practised, evidenced and reviewed routinely
